Name: Salomons Memorial
Short_Description: A stone viewpoint on the crest of Box Hill, the hill’s best-loved outlook, looking over Dorking and the Weald towards the South Downs.
History_or_Lore: Leopold Salomons, a London financier of Norbury Park, purchased 230 acres of Box Hill from the Hope Settled Estates in 1914 for £16,000, after building leases had been proposed on the slopes, and gave the land to the National Trust to keep it open. The stone viewpoint commemorating that gift was unveiled on 16 August 1920 by his widow, Annie Martha Salomons. Its inscription reads: “In grateful remembrance of Leopold Salomons of Norbury Park who gave Box Hill to the Nation 1914.” An orientation stone naming distant landmarks was added in 1922; Salomons himself had called the outlook the “most magnificent in Europe.” This is the classic view of the hill, the country Jane Austen chose for the famous picnic in Emma, where tempers fray in the heat and the landscape seems to look on. The memorial is not a listed building, but it was refurbished and reopened in September 2014 to mark a century of National Trust care. On a clear day the eye can travel as far as Chanctonbury Ring, some twenty-four miles away, with Leith Hill Tower picked out to the west.
Address: Box Hill summit viewpoint, off Zig Zag Road / Box Hill Road, Box Hill, Tadworth, Surrey KT20 7LB (NT Box Hill)
Coord_Source: OSM viewpoint node 'Salomons'

Name: Pine Grove Bridge (site)
Short_Description: The vanished site of one of Lord Lovelace’s 1860s timber-haulage bridges, in woodland near Effingham, where embankments and a few flint and brick blocks still mark the old crossing.
History_or_Lore: In the 1860s William King, 1st Earl of Lovelace, laid out woodland tracks and fifteen brick-and-flint bridges on his East Horsley estate so that horse-drawn carts could carry timber to his sawmill near Brockhole Cross. Most were built with distinctive horseshoe or “Moorish” arches, a romantic flourish in the service of forestry, and they still surprise walkers who come upon them among the trees, like something from a story-book estate. Ten of the fifteen stand; Pine Grove is one of five that do not. It stood in Outdowns Plantation, crossing a bridleway, and the site can still be recognised from the approach embankments and scattered masonry. Sources do not record when or why the bridge was lost. Waymarked trails created by the Horsley Countryside Preservation Society, now the Horsley Heritage Group, link the surviving bridges and the quiet sites of those that have gone.
Address: Woodland near Pine Grove Lodge, on bridleway BW131, Effingham/East Horsley woods, Surrey (nearest postcode KT24 5QR)
Coord_Source: OSM 'Pine Grove Bridge (site of)' node; site only, ~±50 m

Name: Stony Dene Bridge
Short_Description: A Grade II-listed ornamental flint-and-brick Lovelace bridge on the East Horsley–Effingham boundary, its horseshoe arch among the most elaborate of the surviving timber-haulage crossings.
History_or_Lore: Built around 1860 for the Lovelace estate, Stony Dene — also commonly spelled Stoney Dene — is an ornamental horseshoe-arched bridge, brick above a flint and stone rubble base, with retaining walls finished in D-shaped brick coping and corbelled decoration to the arches. Historic England listed it at Grade II in 2000; local heritage accounts give its span as about nine feet. It is one of ten surviving Lovelace Bridges, built so timber could be hauled by horse-drawn carts from the Earl’s woodlands to his sawmill, yet designed with a care that makes the crossing feel almost ceremonial. A major restoration led by the Horsley Countryside Preservation Society began in 2003: the arch was rebuilt, fragments of the original name plaque were found nearby and returned, and the parapets were reconstructed with the aid of a 1950s painting of the bridge. The society records the work as completed in 2011.
Address: Stony Dene Plantation, forest track off Crocknorth Road, Effingham, Surrey (nearest postcode KT24 5QR)
Coord_Source: Historic England NGR TQ1056651747; matches OSM

Name: Horseclose Bridge (site)
Short_Description: The site of a lost Lovelace timber-haulage bridge in Kiln Field Coppice, now marked mainly by the earth embankments that once carried a forestry track over a bridleway.
History_or_Lore: Horseclose Bridge, also written Horse Close, was one of the fifteen brick-and-flint bridges built in the 1860s by William King, 1st Earl of Lovelace, to take horse-drawn timber carts over existing paths on the East Horsley estate. Like Pine Grove, it is one of five Lovelace bridges that no longer stand. Trail descriptions agree that only the embankments remain, with no obvious surviving structure, at the point where the track crossed a bridleway in Kiln Field Coppice. The site lies on the longer Lovelace Bridges trail beyond Stony Dene, towards Meadow Plat, the smallest of the bridges that still survive. Sources do not record when or why Horseclose was removed; the woods have simply closed over the crossing, leaving a fold in the ground for those who know to look. Ten Lovelace bridges remain in the woods around East Horsley and Effingham, and all but one of those survivors are listed at Grade II.
Address: Kiln Field Coppice, on bridleway BW131, East Horsley/Effingham woods, Surrey (nearest postcode KT24 5TG)
Coord_Source: OSM 'Horse Close Bridge (site of)' node; embankments only, ~±50 m

Name: Little Kings Wood Viewpoint
Short_Description: A signed woodland viewpoint on National Trust land in Little Kings Wood, on the North Downs north of Gomshall, looking south towards the Greensand Ridge.
History_or_Lore: Little Kings Wood is a National Trust woodland of about twenty-five hectares on the North Downs escarpment north of Gomshall. A clearly signed viewpoint, listed by Surrey County Council as a highlight of the easy-access walk from Francis Corner on Coombe Lane, opens a gap in the trees towards the Greensand hills that run parallel to the Downs. Independent walk descriptions identify St Martha’s Hill and Leith Hill, Surrey’s highest point, in that view; Holmbury Hill is also reported in the centre. Unlike many neighbouring landmarks, the viewpoint itself has little published history or folklore; its pleasure is quieter, a sudden widening of the woods rather than a named legend. It is reached from the free Coombe Lane car park, on tracks that also connect with the North Downs Way. It sits on the same downs ridge as Ranmore and Wotton, but is more accurately placed above Gomshall than in those valleys.
Address: Little Kings Wood (NT), on bridleway BW134 north of Gomshall, Shere, Surrey; easy-access walk from Francis Corner car park, Coombe Lane
Coord_Source: OSM viewpoint node 'Little Kings Wood viewpoint'

Name: Type 24 Pillbox, Central Wood, Netley Park
Short_Description: One of a line of six Second World War Type 24 pillboxes in the woods above Netley House, built in 1940–41 as part of GHQ Line B to help defend the approaches to London.
History_or_Lore: The National Trust records six brick-and-concrete Type 24 machine-gun emplacements at Netley Park, in the parish of Shere. Each is an irregular hexagon with a doorway in the longer rear wall, embrasures for Bren guns and rifles, and a central Y-shaped blast wall. They were built in 1940–41 as part of GHQ Line B, the anti-tank barrier drawn along the North Downs to protect London. Netley House had already served as a First World War hospital and was occupied by the Canadian army in the Second; the “Canadian road” on the northern boundary is now part of the North Downs Way. Several boxes are set into the hillside, half swallowed by the woods they were meant to command. One close to a path, at about TQ 0805 4853, has an interpretation board by its entrance; another, entered from the rear down a shaft, was cleared with the Pillbox Study Group in 2012, after which a padlocked trapdoor and ladder were fitted. They never fired in anger, but they still startle the walker who finds a gun-slit among the beeches.
Address: Central Wood, Netley Park (NT), on bridleway BW136 above Gomshall, Shere, Surrey (nearest postcode GU5 9QA)
Coord_Source: NT HER NGR TQ 0805 4853 matched to OSM pillbox node

Name: Samuel Wilberforce Memorial
Short_Description: A Grade II-listed granite cross on Abinger Roughs marking the spot where Samuel Wilberforce, Bishop of Winchester, was killed in a riding fall on 19 July 1873.
History_or_Lore: On 19 July 1873 Samuel Wilberforce, son of the abolitionist William Wilberforce and then Bishop of Winchester, was riding from Burford Bridge towards Holmbury St Mary with Lord Granville to visit William Gladstone, when he was thrown from his horse and died almost immediately. The place was then known as Evershed’s Rough, now part of the National Trust’s Abinger Roughs, near Leasers Barn. His family paid for a memorial there. The Illustrated London News in 1874 described a ten-foot granite monolith by Gilliam of Dorking, with a bishop’s pastoral staff across his initials and a floreated cross above. Historic England lists the Celtic-style crucifix at Grade II; the list entry incorrectly gives the date as 12 July. Known as “Soapy Sam” for a smoothness of public manner, he is widely remembered for opposing Darwin’s theory of evolution, and for a celebrated clash with T. H. Huxley at Oxford in 1860. Darwin himself later walked these Roughs as a guest of Thomas Henry Farrer of Abinger Hall. Local ghost lore, recorded by Visit Mole Valley, holds that on the anniversary of the bishop’s death his figure may be seen at the windows of nearby Wotton House.
Address: Beside Abinger Roughs NT car park, White Downs Lane, Abinger Hammer, Surrey RH5 6QS
Coord_Source: Historic England NGR TQ1105448107; matches OSM

Name: The Witches' Broom Tree
Short_Description: A veteran beech on the National Trust’s Abinger Roughs, known locally as the witches’ broom tree, its huge ancient limbs now propped and signed on the estate’s tree trail.
History_or_Lore: The National Trust’s Abinger Roughs tree trail points out an old beech, known locally as the witches’ broom tree, just off the main path, its limbs so ancient that they have to be propped up. Visit Mole Valley describes a gnarled, latticed trunk some nine metres around, thought to be two or three hundred years old, and says the shape is said to resemble a witch’s broom. Some say that mysterious form is simply genetics; others claim it comes from bundle-planting, an old practice of setting several saplings together to yield more timber, so that the stems later fused into one strange body. Look closely, local accounts add, and there is even a part of the trunk that resembles a human skull. Those interpretations are not confirmed in the Trust’s trail text, but they are how the tree is now told in the Surrey Hills. A separate group of veteran sweet chestnuts at The Nower, near Dorking, is recorded as the “Three Sisters”; some locals also call them the “Three Witches.” Charles Darwin walked these Roughs in the 1870s, not far from the tree.
Address: Abinger Roughs (NT), c.300 yards along the tree trail from the car park on White Downs Lane, Abinger Hammer, Surrey RH5 6QS

Name: Blatchford Down
Short_Description: A National Trust stretch of open chalk grassland on the North Downs Way above Abinger, with wide valley views, a grazing-formed habitat for plants and butterflies, and nearby Second World War pillboxes.
History_or_Lore: Blatchford Down, also signed as Blatchford Downs, is National Trust land on the North Downs escarpment, entered through a gate on the North Downs Way between White Down and the slopes above Abinger Roughs. Surrey County Council’s White Down trail describes passing through a kissing gate, then following a grass path downhill past benches with views across chalk grassland and the valley beyond. That open turf was created by grazing in the past, allowing many plants and butterflies to thrive — a bright, windy ledge after the woods. The county trail and the National Trust’s Abinger Roughs to Gomshall walk both record Second World War pillboxes along this stretch of the Way, once commanding clear valley views and now partly screened by trees, reminders that this quiet scarp was once a planned last line before London. Published legend specifically about Blatchford Down is otherwise scarce; it is best understood as part of the wider Hackhurst, White Down and Abinger downs landscape.
Address: North Downs Way / Drove Road, above Abinger Hammer, Surrey (no postcode; nearest RH5 6SF)
Coord_Source: OSM viewpoint node 'Blatchford Down'

Name: Dorking Arch
Short_Description: The largest and most decorative of the surviving Lovelace Bridges, a Grade II-listed flint-and-brick arch spanning Crocknorth Road, the only one of the group clearly visible from a public highway.
History_or_Lore: Dorking Arch was built in the 1860s by William King, 1st Earl of Lovelace, as part of a network of fifteen brick-and-flint bridges that carried horse-drawn timber carts over existing roads and tracks on his East Horsley estate. Historic England listed it at Grade II in 1985. The official list entry describes coursed flint rubble with brick dressings, long ramped retaining walls, bands of billet moulding, and parapets pierced by ten brick-edged lozenge-shaped openings. Local heritage accounts give its span as about eighteen feet, the widest of the Lovelace Bridges, and often describe those openings as decorative arrow slits, as if a forest fortress had been set down over a Surrey lane. Because heavy traffic passes beneath it, vibration is monitored; Horsley Heritage records that significant cracks led, about twenty-five years ago, to strengthening work using concrete injections. Of all the Earl’s crossings, this is the one that still announces itself to the passing world.
Address: Forest track crossing Crocknorth Road, East Horsley, Surrey (nearest postcode KT24 5TF)
Coord_Source: Historic England NGR TQ0997951164

Name: Briary Hill East Bridge
Short_Description: A relatively narrow Grade II-listed Lovelace bridge in the woods at Honeysuckle Bottom, one of a close pair of flint-and-brick arches carrying a former timber track over a bridleway.
History_or_Lore: Briary Hill (East) Bridge was built in the 1860s by the Lovelace Estate so that horse-drawn timber carts could cross existing paths in the woodlands south of East Horsley. Historic England listed it at Grade II in 1985, for group value with the other Lovelace Bridges. The list entry describes a semi-circular brick arch of about seven feet’ span on flint-rubble retaining walls, with D-shaped brick coping, and notes that brick moulding and decoration to the main arch and to the parapets were then largely destroyed. The Horsley Countryside Preservation Society records conservation work in 1981, including reconstruction of the parapets, and places the bridge about 275 metres west of Crocknorth Road along bridleway 103, close to its slightly larger neighbour, Briary Hill West. Come upon the pair in Honeysuckle Bottom and the Earl’s woodland railway of horses and timber still seems only just out of hearing.
Address: Briary Hill, on bridleway BW103 in the woods south of East Horsley, Surrey (nearest postcode KT24 5TG)
Coord_Source: Historic England NGR TQ0995650813

Name: Briary Hill West Bridge
Short_Description: The western of two neighbouring Grade II-listed Lovelace bridges in Honeysuckle Bottom, officially listed as Upper Briary Hill Bridge, with a circular brick arch spanning a woodland bridleway.
History_or_Lore: Officially listed as Upper Briary Hill Bridge, this crossing is now generally known as Briary Hill West. It was built in the 1860s by the Lovelace Estate as one of fifteen flint-and-brick bridges that took timber wagons over existing tracks on the East Horsley estate. Historic England listed it at Grade II in 1985, for group value. The list entry describes a circular brick arch of about ten feet’ span on flint-rubble retaining walls, with D-shaped brick coping and brick voussoirs and moulding to the main arch and to the parapets. Horsley Heritage places it over a bridleway in Coles Copse, some 100 metres down from Briary Hill East and about 240 metres above Raven Arch, and notes a slightly angular alignment over the path. Ten of the original fifteen Lovelace Bridges still stand, unexpected ornaments in the working woods.
Address: Briary Hill (Upper Briary Hill Bridge), woods south of East Horsley, Surrey (nearest postcode KT24 5TG)
Coord_Source: Historic England NGR TQ0985450818

Name: Raven Arch
Short_Description: An easily reached Grade II-listed Lovelace bridge in Honeysuckle Bottom, distinguished by glazed-brick moulding to its semi-circular arch and a recess that once held a name or date plaque.
History_or_Lore: Raven Arch was built in the 1860s by the Lovelace Estate to carry a timber track over a path in Honeysuckle Bottom, East Horsley. Historic England listed it at Grade II in 1985. The list entry describes a semi-circular brick arch of about ten feet’ span on flint-rubble retaining walls, with a glazed-brick four-step moulding to the arches and three-foot parapets. Horsley Heritage notes that the western parapet survives to its full height, with a brick-edged recess for a name or date plaque, and that a decorative arch of black-tipped tiles is the bridge’s most striking feature. It is believed, though not proven, that the name may relate to a heraldic device once displayed on the bridge but no longer preserved. The documented Lovelace arms bear martlets — stylised birds without feet — rather than ravens, so the “raven” may be a lost plaque, a local name, or a misremembered crest. The society carried out conservation from 2007, including restoration of the eastern parapet.
Address: Woodland path in the Lovelace estate woods south of East/West Horsley, Surrey (nearest postcode KT24 5TB)
Coord_Source: Historic England NGR TQ0962551058

Name: GHQ Line Pillboxes near Box Hill Stepping Stones
Short_Description: A Type 24 infantry pillbox, a Type 28 six-pounder anti-tank emplacement and a line of concrete anti-tank cylinders still guard the River Mole below Box Hill, remnants of the 1940 defences of the Dorking Gap.
History_or_Lore: From late June 1940, GHQ Line B was constructed from Farnham along the southern slopes of the North Downs towards Reigate, as an anti-tank barrier to protect London. Dorking was a Class A nodal point at the southern end of the gap through the Downs, a vital route towards the capital; in August 1940 the 3rd Canadian Infantry Brigade was positioned to man these defences. Beside the Mole near the Stepping Stones survive an unusual Type 24 pillbox, built with corrugated-iron shuttering rather than the brick common here, covering the river to the west; a Type 28 six-pounder anti-tank emplacement dug into the south-west facing slope, overlooking the line of an infilled anti-tank ditch; and a row of twelve anti-tank cylinders set at three-foot intervals on a hockey-stick-shaped concrete base along the bank. National Trust records note further concrete cylinders apparently intended to support a barrier across the river itself. A wartime landscape still lies in the grass and the water, only a few yards from the picnic stones.
Address: River Mole riverside path below Box Hill, off Pixham Lane / Stepping Stones car park, Dorking, Surrey (nearest postcode RH4 1PH)
Coord_Source: Type 24 pillbox, NT HER NGR TQ 1748 5095 = OSM bunker node; Type 28 emplacement ~170 m N (51.247198,-0.319437)

Name: GHQ Line Pillboxes on the North Downs Way above Wotton and Ranmore
Short_Description: A scatter of Second World War pillboxes, mostly shell-proof Type 24s, still stands along the North Downs Way on the scarp west of Denbies Hillside and above Wotton and Ranmore, built in 1940 to help defend London.
History_or_Lore: The National Trust notes that concrete pillboxes just west of Denbies Hillside, along the North Downs Way, were built in 1940 to defend London, as positions where an advancing enemy could be engaged before reaching the capital. The Pillbox Study Group records dozens of mostly shell-proof Type 24s between Newlands Corner and Ranmore, with local variations in loopholes, roof edges and entrances fitted to the steep, wooded slopes. One unusual example, just below the path near Wotton at about TQ 121 494, is dug deep into the bank, with a side entrance and the location number 85 still painted in red on its central pillar. Surrey archaeological surveys describe the GHQ Line in this county as following the Tillingbourne to Wotton and the Pipp Brook to Dorking. These defences are distinct from the Netley Park and Blatchford Down groups. Walk the Way in summer and they can seem almost swallowed by hawthorn; in winter they reappear, grey and watchful, along the scarp.
Address: North Downs Way (BW114) on the scarp above Wotton, near God's Seat viewpoint, Surrey
Coord_Source: Group entry: pin = the 'No. 85' pillbox at c. TQ 121 494 (OSM node). Others are spread for several km along the NDW

Name: Leith Hill Tower
Short_Description: An eighteenth-century Gothic folly on the highest point in south-east England, whose spiral steps lead to views that, on a clear day, are said to take in a dozen counties or more.
History_or_Lore: Richard Hull of Leith Hill Place built this Gothic tower in the mid-1760s. Local tradition has long held that he raised it so the hill, just short of a thousand feet, might officially become a mountain. When he died in 1772 he was, at his own request, buried beneath the lower room. Later accounts, including a Francis Frith caption and a BBC feature, say he was buried upside down, so that when the world was turned at the Last Judgement he would face his Maker the right way up; official records confirm only the burial under the tower. The building was later stripped, then repaired and heightened by William Philip Perrin; in 1864 William John Evelyn added the stair turret. The list entry notes that it reputedly commands views of thirteen counties. A further local story has Evelyn turning kangaroos loose on the hill, where they reportedly flourished until they were “exterminated by ruthless individuals.” Visit Mole Valley also tells of ghostly Saxon and Danish armies still marching on the lower slopes towards a battle of 851, though the battlefield itself is uncertain. Hull’s tomb was uncovered during restoration in 1984.
Address: Leith Hill summit, Coldharbour, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6LX (NT Leith Hill)
Coord_Source: Historic England NGR TQ1394843162

Name: Leith Hill Place
Short_Description: A Grade II*-listed country house on the slopes of Leith Hill, long a Wedgwood and Darwin family home and the childhood house of the composer Ralph Vaughan Williams.
History_or_Lore: Leith Hill Place is a house of about 1600, largely rebuilt around 1760 in Palladian style, and listed at Grade II* in 1966. Richard Hull bought the estate in 1754 and built the tower on the hill above. In 1798 it was purchased by William Philip Perrin, who did not live here. The National Trust records that Perrin had inherited five Jamaican sugar plantations, and with them the labour of enslaved people; some of those profits went into buying the estate and raising the tower. In 1847 Josiah Wedgwood III bought the house on retiring from the family pottery; his wife, Caroline Darwin, developed the Rhododendron Wood. Charles Darwin, her brother, often stayed and experimented in the grounds. Their daughter Margaret was the mother of Ralph Vaughan Williams, who spent his childhood here, was taught the piano by his aunt Sophy, and later wrote music steeped in this landscape, including The Lark Ascending. On inheriting the estate in 1944 he gave the house and grounds to the National Trust. The tower had already been in the Trust’s care since 1923.
Address: Leith Hill Lane, Forest Green, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6LY
Coord_Source: Historic England NGR TQ1338342362

Name: Darwin's Worm Stone
Short_Description: A stone in the grounds of Leith Hill Place that Charles Darwin watched sinking slowly into the soil, evidence he used in his last book on the quiet, enormous work of earthworms.
History_or_Lore: Charles Darwin frequently visited his sister Caroline Wedgwood at Leith Hill Place and carried out experiments in the grounds, often with his nieces Sophy, Margaret and Lucy. He noticed that earth had begun to bank up against the sides of one stone, and that the stone itself was sinking, year by year, as if the ground were gently swallowing it. He concluded that earthworms were excavating soil from beneath it and depositing it on the surface, and believed that ancient ruins became buried in the same way — a scientific fable that happens to be true. The work contributed to his final book, The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms. The National Trust records that Darwin’s “worm stone” still lies in the grounds, beside a waymarker for the orange trail below the house. There is no ghost here, only the slowest of wonders: a stone going into the earth by the labour of worms, just as Darwin said it would.
Address: Grounds of Leith Hill Place (NT), below the house beside the orange-trail waymarker, Leith Hill Lane, Dorking RH5 6LY

Name: Box Hill Fort
Short_Description: A scheduled late-Victorian London mobilisation centre, known locally as the Old Fort, whose earth-sheltered magazines and crescent-shaped blast bank still sit near the National Trust visitor centre on Box Hill.
History_or_Lore: Box Hill Fort is one of the London mobilisation centres built in the 1890s under the London Defence Positions, a scheme drawn up in 1888 to protect the capital from invasion. Fifteen such centres were planned along a seventy-two-mile stop-line; Box Hill’s compound, built around 1890, was to store ammunition and tools and serve as a point around which trenches could be thrown up in a crisis. Official confidence in the navy had been restored by 1905 and the scheme was abandoned, with land sales beginning in 1907, so the fort never had its war. The scheduled remains include a reinforced-concrete and brick structure of magazines and stores, with a large crescent-shaped earthen blast-bank and outer ditch to the rear. The former caretaker’s lodge and tool store nearby now serve as the visitor centre. Bats occupy the fort, which can be viewed from outside but not entered. It sits close to Major Labelliere’s grave, so that Victorian precaution and Georgian eccentricity share the same hilltop.
Address: Near Box Hill NT visitor centre, Zig Zag Road, Box Hill, Tadworth, Surrey KT20 7LB
Coord_Source: OSM 'The Old Fort' building way (scheduled monument)

Name: Broadwood's Folly
Short_Description: A Grade II-listed circular flint tower on Lodge Hill, Box Hill, a fairytale eye-catcher built by the piano-maker Thomas Broadwood, and said by some to mark the Battle of Waterloo.
History_or_Lore: The Broadwood Folly at Juniper Hall was built around 1815 on Lodge Hill by Thomas Broadwood, of the piano-manufacturing family, after he purchased Juniper Hall in the valley below. Historic England listed the circular flint tower, about eight metres high and with a decorative machicolated parapet, at Grade II in 2005. The list entry records a blocked east door, other openings, and the settings of a lost spiral stair that once led to views from the top. Headley and Meulenkamp state that the tower was built as a Waterloo memorial, and Visit Mole Valley notes that it is said by some to have been raised to mark that battle; the claim is traditional rather than proven, but it has clung to the tower. A vista once ran north through an avenue of beeches to Juniper Hall; the trees were lost in the gale of 1987. A holm oak later grew up through the centre of the tower, a green spire in a flint crown, and had in the end to be cut down. The Trust has considered conservation, including rebuilding the staircase.
Address: Juniper Hall estate, off Juniper Bottom / Zig Zag Road, Mickleham, Dorking, Surrey (nearest postcode RH5 6BN)
Coord_Source: OSM building way tagged HE 1391454; matches HE NGR TQ176522

Name: Box Hill Stepping Stones
Short_Description: A well-loved crossing of the River Mole at the foot of Box Hill, first recorded in the nineteenth century, removed in the Second World War, and formally reopened in 1946 by Clement Attlee.
History_or_Lore: The Stepping Stones cross the Mole at Burford Bridge, Westhumble, on National Trust land, and today form part of the North Downs Way; they formerly marked the Pilgrims’ Way. A crossing is believed to have existed here for centuries. The stones themselves are first recorded in 1841, when, some local accounts suggest, they may have been laid by the then owner of Burford Lodge. There are seventeen hexagonal stones. The National Trust records that they were removed during the Second World War in case of invasion. James Chuter Ede, then Home Secretary, who had known the crossing since his schooldays in Dorking, encouraged their reinstatement and himself paid the bill of £156 19s 6d, “considerably higher than I expected,” in thanks for what the town had done for him in boyhood. On 11 September 1946, his sixty-fourth birthday, he invited Prime Minister Clement Attlee to reopen them. In the car park a concrete slab, built by Canadian forces in 1944, was used to waterproof and test military vehicles before D-Day, driving them through the river and back again. Nearby, wartime concrete cylinders still hint at a barrier that once, or was meant to, close the Mole.
Address: River Mole, footpath from Stepping Stones NT car park off the A24 / Old London Road, Westhumble, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6AE
Coord_Source: OSM stepping_stones node

Name: Betchworth Castle
Short_Description: A scheduled and Grade II-listed ruin of a medieval fortified manor house on a sandstone spur above the Mole, between Dorking and Brockham, later reduced to a picturesque landscape feature — and thick with ghost lore.
History_or_Lore: Betchworth Castle was the fortified manor of West Betchworth, on a spur overlooking the Mole. Dorking Museum records a licence to crenellate and impark in 1379, when the Arundel family held the manor; the scheduled monument entry dates that licence to 1377. A second licence followed in 1448 for Sir Thomas Browne. The standing sandstone and brick ruins belong mainly to later medieval and Tudor phases. Local tradition adds that Edward I stayed here on 14 May 1294, on his way to Chichester. In the 1690s William Fenwick reduced much of the house. Henry Thomas Hope bought the park for Deepdene in 1834, for £19,000, and dismantled part of what remained to leave a romantic ruin in a former deer park said once to have covered 360 acres. Visit Mole Valley and other local accounts say the ruins are haunted by a black dog that prowls by night. Legend also tells of “Lord Hope” chasing an escaped prisoner in the dark and running his own son through by mistake; it is the father’s anguished ghost, wringing his hands, that is said to walk here, not the slain son. Conservation in the 2010s has secured the standing remains, now railed.
Address: Off Castle Gardens, Brockham, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1NY
Coord_Source: OSM historic=castle node; ruin on private land, view from public footpath

Name: William Mullins House
Short_Description: A jettied house on West Street, Dorking, marked by a blue plaque as the home of the Mayflower passenger William Mullins, and widely described as the only known surviving home of a Pilgrim Father.
History_or_Lore: The house at 58–61 West Street, now a café, has been dendrochronologically dated by Dorking Museum to 1589. William Mullins, a shoemaker, bought it in 1612 and sold it in 1619. He was not one of the separatist “Saints” who initiated the Mayflower voyage, but one of the “Strangers” recruited to help fund it. In July 1620 he embarked with his wife Alice, their children Priscilla and Joseph, and their servant Robert Carter. Mayflower 400 records that this shoemaker, intending to set up in the new colony, took 265 pairs of shoes and boots with him. William, Alice, Joseph and Carter all died in the first winter; only teenage Priscilla survived. She later married the cooper John Alden. A later literary tradition, made famous by Longfellow’s The Courtship of Miles Standish, has Captain Standish sending Alden to propose on his behalf, only for Priscilla to say, “Why don’t you speak for yourself, John?” Historians treat the love triangle as unverified; the marriage itself is fact. The museum and Mayflower 400 describe the house as the only home of a “Pilgrim Father” known to have survived. A blue plaque marks the front.
Address: 58 West Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1BS

Name: Dorking War Memorial
Short_Description: A Grade II-listed Portland stone memorial on South Street, an imposing classical aedicule unveiled in 1921 for Dorking’s First World War dead and later extended for those who died in the Second.
History_or_Lore: The memorial, listed in 2008, was designed by Thomas Braddock, who had won a competition, and was unveiled on 17 July 1921 before a crowd of about 3,000. It stands on a raised platform against a retaining wall, an aedicule with pilasters, a moulded cornice and a triangular pediment. Three panels name the fallen, under the heading “IN MEMORY OF DORKING MEN WHO FELL IN THE GREAT WAR”; the plinth quotes 1 Samuel 25:16, and the pilasters bear roundels dated 1914 and 1919. Dorking Museum records 269 names on the town memorial, listed without regard to rank. The original scheme included a bandstand, iron railings and wooden seating. The railings were taken for the war effort in the Second World War; after 1945 the seating was removed and low walls were added on either side, naming those who died between 1939 and 1945. There is no need of a ghost story here: the names, and the scar where the railings were cut away, are memorial enough. The entrance to the South Street Caves lies immediately beside it.
Address: South Street, Dorking, Surrey (nearest postcode RH4 2LD)

Name: Druid's Grove, Norbury Park
Short_Description: A steep yew woodland in Norbury Park, across the Mole from Box Hill, whose ancient trees are among the most celebrated in the Surrey Hills, though the Druid name is a romantic invention.
History_or_Lore: Druid’s Grove lies on the steep slopes of Norbury Park. The yew-and-box woodland of this stretch of the North Downs is a rare habitat, part of a Special Area of Conservation. Surrey Wildlife Trust notes that the yews may be up to 3,000 years old; that figure is an estimate, not a measured date. The Ancient Yew Group has recorded several of the largest trees here, with girths of around 18 to 22 feet. The name was not mapped until the 1873 Ordnance Survey, though earlier writers spoke of a “Druids’ Walk.” There is no reliable evidence that the grove was a Druid sanctuary; the title is a Victorian romantic label for a sombre, aged place. George Meredith, who lived nearby, told visitors that anyone walking under the yews should remember they were saplings when Jesus Christ came to earth. A visitor in 1878 wrote of ghostly trees like conscious creatures, and of trunks that awakened “long-forgotten stories of huge hairy giants.” In 1931 Surrey County Council bought Norbury Park to prevent its development. The park is a Grade II registered landscape, laid out in the picturesque taste by William Lock in the late eighteenth century.
Address: Norbury Park, west of Mickleham, on paths from Westhumble / Crabtree Lane, Surrey (nearest postcode RH5 6BQ)

Name: Major Peter Labelliere's Grave
Short_Description: A stone on Box Hill marks the burial of Major Peter Labelliere, a Dorking eccentric who asked to be interred head downwards — and whose ghost, local lore says, still roams the hill.
History_or_Lore: Near Box Hill Fort a stone commemorates Major Peter Labelliere (also Labilliere), “buried here head downwards 11th July 1800.” He left instructions to be buried upside down, because the world was topsy-turvy and he wanted to be right in the end. His devotions suggest another motive: a wish to emulate St Peter, traditionally crucified inverted. Timbs called him an officer of marines, and told of a rejected love and a cottage named “The Hole in the Wall” on Butter Hill. Local anecdote adds that he predicted the day of his death, and asked that his landlady’s youngest children dance upon his coffin; only the boy complied. A great crowd attended the funeral; mischievous persons are said to have removed the wooden bridge over the Mole, so that many had to wade home. The present stone says 11 July; a 1928 photograph of an earlier stone is said to show 11 June. A later reburial in consecrated ground remains uncertain. Visit Mole Valley and Surrey folklore hold that his sword-wielding ghost still roams the summit. John Janaway recorded an aunt who believed she met him in a thunderstorm: a one-eyed man in a long coat and three-cornered hat, who suddenly disappeared.
Address: Box Hill, short walk west of the NT visitor centre, Zig Zag Road, Tadworth, Surrey KT20 7LB

Name: Hope Mausoleum
Short_Description: A Grade II*-listed Greek Revival mausoleum on the former Deepdene estate, built in 1818 for the collector Thomas Hope, later buried from sight, and now the principal surviving building associated with him.
History_or_Lore: Thomas Hope, the art collector and champion of the Neo-Classical style, bought The Deepdene in 1807. In 1817 his youngest son, Charles, died of a fever in Rome, aged seven. The following year Hope built this mausoleum on the edge of Chart Park, over the burial place of the boy’s ashes, probably to designs by William Atkinson with Hope’s own input. The ashlar building has a pedimented antechamber and a vaulted burial chamber, set into the hillside behind a railed courtyard. Hope was buried here in 1831, “in the quietest manner next to that of my ever lamented son Charles.” The last interment was that of the 8th Duke of Newcastle in 1941. After vandalism the entrance was sealed in 1957; between 1960 and 1973 the structure itself was buried, a lost tomb in the woods, until it was uncovered and restored as part of the Deepdene Trail. The Deepdene house was demolished in 1969. No separate ghost is firmly attached to the mausoleum; the darker Hope legend belongs to Betchworth Castle, where “Lord Hope” is said to wander, wringing his hands.
Address: Deepdene Wood, off Chart Lane South / Deepdene Trail, Dorking, Surrey RH5 4DA

Name: St Barnabas Church, Ranmore
Short_Description: A Grade II*-listed flint estate church on Ranmore Common, designed in 1859 by Sir George Gilbert Scott for George Cubitt of Denbies, its tall octagonal spire a landmark on the ridge.
History_or_Lore: St Barnabas was built in 1859 by Sir George Gilbert Scott for George Cubitt, later first Lord Ashcombe and son of the builder Thomas Cubitt. Scott, a leading Gothic Revival architect, was a friend of Cubitt and a frequent visitor to nearby Denbies, the family house demolished in 1954, so that the church now outlives the great house it was built to serve. It is cruciform, of flint cobbles with ashlar dressings, with a large central octagonal tower and a tall facetted spire that can be seen for miles along the downs. The richly finished interior uses coloured marble and alabaster. The south transept became a memorial chapel, with a war memorial erected in 1920 by the second Baron Ashcombe for his three sons killed in the First World War, and painted by the late Pre-Raphaelite artist Reginald Frampton. In 1962, after the death of the third Baron, patronage passed to the Church Commissioners and the church was united with St Martin’s, Dorking. First Lord Ashcombe is buried east of the chancel.
Address: Ranmore Common Road, Ranmore Common, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6SP

Name: Burford Bridge Hotel
Short_Description: A Grade II-listed former coaching inn at the foot of Box Hill, long associated with Nelson, Keats and Hazlitt, and still wrapped in literary rumour and a little ghost lore.
History_or_Lore: Burford Bridge Hotel, originally the Fox and Hounds, is an early-nineteenth-century L-shaped building of roughcast under a slate roof, listed at Grade II in 1973. The official list entry records that Nelson stayed here on his last night in England on his way to Portsmouth before Trafalgar; that Keats wrote the last part of Endymion here in 1819; and that William Hazlitt also stayed. Keats’s own letters place him at the inn in late November 1817, when he finished Endymion after climbing Box Hill “after the Moon,” and some later historians have also doubted the Trafalgar-eve timing of Nelson’s visit. Local accounts nonetheless keep both stories close, and add Emma, Lady Hamilton, Wordsworth, Stevenson and even Queen Victoria to the guest-roll. Jane Austen, who knew this stretch of country, set a famous picnic on Box Hill in Emma. Ghost-lore listings tell of Lord Nelson’s coachman, reportedly seen in a long coat near the old stables and car park. Adjoining the main range are contemporary stables, and a seventeenth-century barn from Abinger, re-erected here, according to the list, in 1934.
Address: Old London Road, Mickleham, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6BX

Name: Westhumble Chapel
Short_Description: The flint ruins of a small medieval chapel of ease at Westhumble, a scheduled monument and Grade II listed building on National Trust land, standing on an old pilgrim route towards Ranmore.
History_or_Lore: West Humble Chapel, on Chapel Lane, is a small rectangular medieval building of which the west gable, part of the east wall and the lower part of the south wall still stand, built of coursed flint and sandstone. The Grade II list entry describes it as a late-thirteenth-century chapel on the Pilgrims’ Way; National Trust and earlier archaeological accounts suggest it may have originated in the late twelfth century as a chapel of ease to Mickleham. The aisleless nave and chancel were about sixteen metres long. The chapel was possibly abandoned around 1500, and certainly before about 1540 on coin evidence, and was later used as a farm building. Clearance and slight restoration in the 1930s revealed associated burials. The remains are both listed and scheduled, a rare fragment of a medieval chapel in Surrey. No distinct ghost story is firmly attached to the ruin, but the place has the atmosphere that such stories like: a broken west gable on an old pilgrim road, graves found again in the last century, and the downs rising behind towards Box Hill and Ranmore.
Address: Chapel Lane, Westhumble, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6AY

Name: St Martin's Church, Dorking
Short_Description: Dorking’s Grade II*-listed parish church, rebuilt by Henry Woodyer in 1868–77, is crowned by a 210-foot tower and spire begun under Bishop Samuel Wilberforce and completed as his memorial.
History_or_Lore: St Martin’s was rebuilt in knapped flint and ashlar between 1868 and 1877 to designs by Henry Woodyer, in a fourteenth-century Gothic manner, with a later Lady Chapel of 1905–13. The foundation stone of the four-stage west tower was laid on 29 May 1873 by Samuel Wilberforce, Bishop of Winchester. Less than two months later he was killed in a riding fall on Abinger Roughs, and the tower and spire were built as the “Wilberforce Memorial.” The top stone of the spire was set on 25 April 1877. The church’s own account gives the height to the weather vane, a Dorking cockerel, as 210 feet. That five-toed bird is the town’s old emblem, and the gilded cockerel turning on the spire has become one of the valley’s familiar signs, a landmark for many miles. Historic England lists the church at Grade II*. The interior is richly fitted, with stained glass and mural decoration by Arthur Powell, and the porch holds a bronze memorial to Ralph Vaughan Williams, who knew this town and these hills from childhood at Leith Hill Place.
Address: Church Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1DW

Name: St John the Evangelist, Wotton
Short_Description: A Grade I-listed village church of Saxon and Norman origin, with a late-seventeenth-century mortuary chapel containing the plain coffin-shaped tombs of the diarist John Evelyn and his wife Mary.
History_or_Lore: The Church of St John the Evangelist, Wotton, was listed at Grade I in 1966. Historic England describes it as probably of Saxon origin, with mid-eleventh-century Norman nave wall and tower, and thirteenth-century chancel, north chapel, north aisle and nave. The Evelyn Mortuary Chapel on the north is of late seventeenth-century thin brick. Among the monuments, the list entry records two unornamented coffin-shaped slabs to John Evelyn, 1706, and his wife, 1709. A seventeenth-century screen of 1632, noted as one of the few of that period to survive in Surrey, stands between the north aisle and chapel. The list entry adds that some trees in the churchyard were reputedly planted by John Evelyn himself. No haunting is firmly recorded in the church; the ghost stories belong to nearby Wotton House, once the Evelyn family seat. Visit Mole Valley relates that firefighters sent to a blaze there in the 1960s claimed to see a ghostly figure carrying fishing gear in the night-time grounds, and that the ghost of Bishop Samuel Wilberforce may be spotted at the house’s front windows on the anniversary of his death.
Address: Church Lane, off Guildford Road (A25), Wotton, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6QQ

Name: South Street Caves
Short_Description: A remarkable set of man-made sand caves beside Dorking’s war memorial, probably begun as an underground folly, later used as wine vaults, and long embroidered with stories of dissenters, smugglers and a hidden river.
History_or_Lore: Dorking stands on Folkestone Sands, underlain by many cellars and caves. The South Street Caves were probably dug in the late seventeenth century. Dorking Museum notes that some have suggested they were used for secret political meetings or as a refuge for religious dissenters, but considers it more likely they were excavated as a folly, when Charles Howard at the Deepdene and John Evelyn at Albury created similar underground features. A carved date of 1666 is recorded, though one specialist considers that graffiti unreliable; a well is said to bear 1672 as part of a hex charm to stop evil rising to the surface. The lowest room is locally called the “Mystery Chamber,” a circular hollow with a stone bench, which some think may have served a dissenting group. John Timbs, in 1822, described a cave on Butter Hill, reached by fifty steps to a “crystalline spring,” and said its creator wasted his fortune on the digging and died in the poor house — a story later writers find unproven. The lower chamber later attracted “increasingly improbable stories of smugglers and a hidden river.” Wine bins from 1815 could hold 700 bottles. The museum has run public tours since 2015.
Address: Entrance in South Street next to the war memorial, Dorking, Surrey (nearest postcode RH4 2LD)
